framing: Follow one prompt from token IDs to the next word
paragraphs: A language model can look impossibly large from the outside. Inside, it repeats a short recipe: positions read from each other, each position updates its own features, and the result feeds the next round. Once you can follow that recipe through one small prompt, the size of a real model stops being intimidating.

We will trace one query through a weighted read by hand, watch the shapes stay fixed through the blocks, and see where the vocabulary finally enters. Shapes turn out to be a debugging tool, because they tell you which operations let positions interact and which work inside a single row.

The property to hold onto is causality. A state that predicts a later word may depend only on what came before it, and you can test that directly: change a future token and check that earlier outputs stay exactly the same. That one test catches a bug that can otherwise pass for a great training run.

Our small model uses weights we wrote by hand, so you can read every number. It knows nothing about English, and that is fine. The goal is to understand the calculation, so that an attention mask or the output layer becomes a specific part you can inspect.
outcomes: Trace queries, keys, and values through one weighted read.
Explain multi-head shapes, residual additions, and where normalization goes.
Connect a causal block to vocabulary probabilities, and test that the future cannot leak.
question: Where could future information get into a decoder, and what test would catch it?
